q: What is Spring Framework, in one sentence?
o: A CSS library used to style web pages and components
A Java framework whose container creates beans and wires them together
A database engine that stores and queries relational data
A build tool that compiles and packages Java projects
e:
Spring is a very large Java framework. Its heart is the "IoC container" (Inversion of Control): instead of your code doing `new` and wiring everything by hand, Spring creates the objects, called beans, and gives each class the other objects it needs.
On top of that core it offers modules for web (Spring MVC), database access (Spring Data), security (Spring Security), transactions, testing and more.
r: Spring = container that builds and wires your objects.
fa: A Java framework whose core idea is a container that creates your objects (beans) and connects them to each other (dependency injection)

q: What does Spring Boot add on top of Spring?
o: It replaces Java with a simpler language
It adds auto-configuration, starters and an embedded server
It adds a graphical interface for designing Spring apps
It introduces a new programming language for Spring
e:
Plain Spring needs a lot of manual configuration (XML or Java config, choosing library versions, deploying a WAR to a separate server).
Spring Boot makes sensible default choices:
- Starters: one dependency (`spring-boot-starter-web`) brings a compatible set of libraries.
- Auto-configuration: if it sees a library on the classpath, it configures it for you.
- Embedded server (Tomcat by default): the app is a normal JAR you start with `java -jar`.
- Actuator: health and metrics endpoints.
r: Spring Boot = Spring with defaults, starters and an embedded server.
fa: Auto-configuration, starter dependencies and an embedded server, so you can run a production-ready app with minimal setup

q: What is Dependency Injection (DI)?
o: A class builds every object that it needs with `new`
A class declares needs and a container provides them
Copying a database table into a different schema
A technique to inject JavaScript code into web pages
e:
Without DI, `OrderService` would write `new PaymentGateway()` inside itself, so it is tied to that exact class and hard to test.
With DI, `OrderService` receives a `PaymentGateway` (usually an interface) through its constructor. Spring decides which implementation to give.
Benefits: loose coupling, easy replacement, and in unit tests you can pass a fake or mock.
r: Don't create your dependencies; receive them.
fa: A class declares what it needs and an external container provides those objects, usually through the constructor

q: Which injection style is generally recommended in Spring?
o: Field injection with `@Autowired` on fields
Constructor injection with final fields
Setter injection on every optional bean
Static fields that are set by the container
e:
Constructor injection is preferred because:
- Dependencies can be `final`, so the object is always fully built.
- It is obvious what a class needs (look at the constructor).
- Unit tests can create the class with `new` and pass mocks, without Spring.
- Circular dependencies show up immediately.
Field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection or Spring to test. With a single constructor you do not even need `@Autowired`.
r: Prefer constructor injection.
fa: Constructor injection

q: What do `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@RestController` have in common?
o: They are all annotations used only inside test classes
Stereotypes: Spring detects them and registers beans
They only work when placed on interfaces, not on classes
They create the matching database tables at startup
e:
`@Component` is the generic marker: "Spring, please manage this class" (component scanning finds it).
`@Service` marks business logic, `@Repository` marks data access (it also translates persistence exceptions into Spring's exceptions), and `@RestController` marks a web controller that returns data (JSON) instead of views.
They behave like `@Component`, but names communicate the architecture.
r: Stereotypes = "manage this class as a bean" + layer meaning.
fa: They are stereotype annotations that tell Spring to detect the class and register it as a bean; the last three add meaning to a layer

q: What is the default scope of a Spring bean?
o: Prototype: a new instance on every injection
Singleton: one shared instance per application context
Request: one instance for each HTTP request
Session: one instance for each logged-in user
e:
By default Spring creates ONE instance of each bean and shares it everywhere (singleton scope; not the GoF pattern, but one per container).
Because many threads use the same object, singleton beans should be stateless: avoid mutable fields that change per request.
Other scopes exist (`prototype`, `request`, `session`) but are rarely needed.
r: Beans are singletons by default, so keep them stateless.

q: What is the purpose of `@SpringBootApplication`?
o: It starts the database that the application will use
It combines configuration, auto-config and component scan
It defines a REST endpoint directly on the main class
It runs the unit tests when the application starts
e:
Placed on your main class, it is a shortcut for three annotations:
- `@Configuration`: the class can define beans.
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration`: turn on Spring Boot's automatic setup.
- `@ComponentScan`: scan this package and sub-packages for `@Component`, `@Service`...
That is why the main class should live in the top-level package of your project.
r: Main class annotation = config + auto-config + component scan.
fa: It combines `@Configuration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration` and `@ComponentScan`, marking the main class of the app

q: What does this endpoint do?
o: Answers `GET /api/users/42` with the user as JSON
Answers `POST /api/users` and creates a new user
Reads `id` from the JSON body of the request
Deletes the user that has the id in the path
e:
`@RestController` means every method returns data written directly to the HTTP response body (Spring converts the object to JSON with Jackson).
`@RequestMapping("/api/users")` gives the base path, `@GetMapping("/{id}")` handles GET requests, and `@PathVariable` takes the value from the URL.
So `GET /api/users/42` calls `get(42)`.
r: @PathVariable = from the URL path. @RequestParam = from ?query. @RequestBody = from the body.
fa: Responds to `GET /api/users/42` with the user serialized as JSON, where `id` = 42

q: Which annotation reads a JSON request body into a Java object?
o: `@PathVariable`
`@RequestParam`
`@RequestBody`
`@ResponseBody`
e:
`@RequestBody` tells Spring to read the HTTP body (usually JSON) and convert it into the Java parameter with Jackson.
`@RequestParam` reads query parameters (`/search?name=ana`), `@PathVariable` reads parts of the path.
`@ResponseBody` is the opposite direction (object to body); `@RestController` already applies it to all methods.
r: Body = @RequestBody. Query = @RequestParam. Path = @PathVariable.

q: Where do you usually put settings such as the database URL in Spring Boot, and how do you switch between environments?
o: Hard-coded in the Java classes, changed by recompiling
In `application.yml`, with `spring.profiles.active`
Only in `pom.xml`, inside the dependencies section
In the browser, sent along with each user request
e:
Spring Boot reads configuration from `application.properties` or `application.yml` in `src/main/resources`.
For different environments you create profile files like `application-dev.yml` and `application-prod.yml` and activate one with `spring.profiles.active=prod` (or the `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` environment variable).
Secrets (passwords, API keys) should not be committed: override them with environment variables or a secrets manager.
ec:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/app
    username: app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}   # from an environment variable
r: Config in application.yml, per-environment via profiles, secrets via env vars.
fa: In `application.properties` or `application.yml`, with profiles (`application-dev.yml`, `application-prod.yml`) activated by `spring.profiles.active`

q: What does Spring Boot auto-configuration do?
o: It rewrites your code automatically while compiling
It reads the classpath and registers default beans
It downloads any missing libraries while running
It formats your code to match the Spring style
e:
Auto-configuration classes are conditional: "if class X is on the classpath and no bean of type Y exists, create Y".
Example: add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` and a PostgreSQL driver, set the URL in properties, and Spring Boot creates the `DataSource`, `EntityManagerFactory` and transaction manager for you.
If you define your own bean of that type, the auto-configured one backs off. To see what happened, run with `--debug`.
r: Auto-config = conditional defaults that back off when you provide your own.
fa: It inspects the classpath and your properties and registers sensible beans automatically (e.g. a DataSource if a JDBC driver is present), backing off if you define your own

q: What is the difference between `@Component` and `@Bean`?
o: There is no difference; both register a bean the same way
`@Component` scans your class; `@Bean` uses a method result
`@Bean` is meant for tests only, not for production code
`@Component` can only be placed on interfaces, not classes
e:
`@Component` (and its stereotypes) annotates your own class, and Spring discovers it by component scanning.
`@Bean` is placed on a method in a `@Configuration` class. The returned object is registered as a bean. Use it when you cannot annotate the class (a library class like `ObjectMapper` or `RestClient`) or when construction needs custom logic.
r: @Component = my class. @Bean = a factory method for any class.
fa: `@Component` goes on a class you own and is found by scanning; `@Bean` goes on a method inside a `@Configuration` class and registers the returned object, useful for third-party classes

q: What happens if two beans of the same type exist and you inject that type without more information?
o: Spring picks one of the beans at random for you
Startup fails (NoUniqueBeanDefinition); use `@Primary`
Spring injects both of the beans into the same field
Nothing fails, and the field is injected as null
e:
If `PaymentGateway` has two implementations (`StripeGateway`, `PaypalGateway`), Spring cannot know which one you want and fails at startup (good: you find out immediately).
Fixes: mark one as `@Primary` (default choice), use `@Qualifier("stripeGateway")` at the injection point, or inject `List<PaymentGateway>` / `Map<String, PaymentGateway>` if you want all of them.
r: Ambiguity => @Primary or @Qualifier.
fa: Startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; resolve it with `@Primary` or `@Qualifier`

q: What does `@Transactional` do?
o: It makes the method run faster by caching the results
It wraps the method in a transaction: commit or rollback
It makes the method run asynchronously in another thread
It encrypts the data that the method reads and writes
e:
A transaction groups several database operations so they all succeed or all fail (ACID). `@Transactional` does this declaratively: Spring starts a transaction before the method and commits after it.
Default rollback rule: only for unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error). A checked exception does NOT roll back unless you write `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`.
Place it on service methods (the unit of work), not on controllers or repositories.
r: @Transactional: commit on success, rollback on RuntimeException by default.
fa: Wraps the method in a database transaction: commit if it completes, roll back if a RuntimeException (or Error) escapes

q: Why might `@Transactional` NOT work in this code?
o: Because the method is public and it must be private
Transactions use a proxy; a call within the class skips it
Because `@Transactional` only ever works on interfaces
Because the method has no parameters declared in it
e:
Spring does not change your class. It wraps the bean in a proxy object that starts and commits the transaction around the call.
When an outside class calls `reportService.saveAll()`, it goes through the proxy and works. But when `generate()` calls `saveAll()` inside the same object, it is a normal Java call on `this`, so the proxy is skipped and there is no transaction.
Same problem with `private` or `final` methods. Fix: move the method to another bean, or put `@Transactional` on the method called from outside.
r: Self-invocation and private methods bypass Spring's proxy.
fa: Because Spring applies transactions through a proxy, and a call from another method of the same class (self-invocation) bypasses the proxy

q: What does a Spring Data JPA repository interface give you?
o: Nothing until you write the SQL for every single method
Ready-made CRUD methods and queries from method names
Only read operations, with no way of saving any data
A web page to browse the data stored in the database
e:
You only declare an interface. At startup Spring Data creates the implementation for you.
`JpaRepository<User, Long>` gives CRUD methods, paging and sorting. Method names like `findByEmail` or `findByAgeGreaterThanAndActiveTrue` are parsed and turned into queries automatically (derived queries).
For complicated queries, use `@Query("select ...")` with JPQL or native SQL.
r: Declare the interface; Spring writes the implementation.
fa: Ready-made CRUD methods (`save`, `findById`, `findAll`, `deleteById`) plus queries generated from method names such as `findByEmail`

q: In JPA, what do `@Entity` and `@Id` mean?
o: `@Entity` marks a class mapped to a table; `@Id` marks the primary key
`@Entity` is a REST controller; `@Id` is a URL parameter
`@Entity` creates a bean; `@Id` is the id of a thread
Both only change how the class is written to the logs
e:
JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is the standard for mapping Java objects to relational tables (ORM). Hibernate is the most popular implementation.
`@Entity` says: instances of this class are rows of a table. `@Id` marks the primary key field. `@GeneratedValue` lets the database generate it, `@Column` customizes a column.
Every entity needs a no-argument constructor (can be protected) because the provider creates objects by reflection.
r: @Entity = table row object. @Id = primary key.
fa: `@Entity` marks a Java class that maps to a table; `@Id` marks the field that is the primary key

q: What is the difference between LAZY and EAGER fetching in JPA?
o: LAZY loads on first access; EAGER loads with the parent
LAZY is always faster, while EAGER is always slower
LAZY deletes the related data, while EAGER saves it
There is no difference at all between the two modes
e:
A `User` may have many `Order`s. With EAGER, loading a user also loads all their orders right away, even if you never use them. With LAZY, orders are loaded from the database only when you first call `user.getOrders()`.
Defaults: `@OneToMany` is LAZY, `@ManyToOne` is EAGER.
LAZY avoids loading too much, but accessing a lazy field after the session/transaction has closed throws `LazyInitializationException`. A common recommendation is to use LAZY and fetch what you need explicitly (`JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph`).
r: Prefer LAZY, fetch explicitly what a use case needs.
fa: LAZY loads related data only when you first access it; EAGER loads it immediately together with the parent

q: What is the N+1 problem in JPA and how do you fix it?
o: It means the database has N+1 tables in its schema
One query for N parents, then one per parent: `JOIN FETCH`
It means the application uses N+1 threads in total
It is a syntax error that JPQL reports at startup
e:
Example: `findAll()` loads 100 users (1 query). Then your code loops and calls `user.getOrders()`, which is LAZY, so JPA runs 1 query per user: 100 more. Total 101 queries instead of 1 or 2.
Fixes: `select u from User u join fetch u.orders` loads everything with one JOIN; `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "orders")` on the repository method; `@BatchSize` to load children in groups; or a DTO projection that selects only what you need.
Detect it by turning on SQL logging and counting queries.
ec:
@Query("select u from User u join fetch u.orders")
List<User> findAllWithOrders();
r: N+1 = 1 query for parents + 1 per child. Fetch join solves it.
fa: One query loads N parents, then one extra query per parent loads its children (N+1 queries total). Fix with `JOIN FETCH`, `@EntityGraph` or batch fetching

q: What is the persistence context and what is "dirty checking"?
o: A log file where the database records its changes
A per-transaction entity cache; changes saved at commit
A security feature that limits who can read an entity
A way to copy tables from one database to another
e:
When you load an entity inside a transaction, JPA keeps it in a persistence context (first-level cache) and remembers its original values. This entity is "managed".
If you call a setter on a managed entity, then at flush/commit JPA detects the difference (dirty checking) and runs the `UPDATE` itself. So inside a `@Transactional` method, `user.setName("x")` is enough; `save()` is not required.
The same `findById` twice in one transaction also returns the same object without hitting the database again.
r: Managed entities are auto-saved at commit when changed.
fa: A per-transaction cache of managed entities; at commit, JPA compares them with their original state and issues UPDATEs automatically for changed ones, even without calling `save`

q: What is the role of `@ControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler`?
o: It authenticates the users before each controller call
It centralizes exception handling and HTTP error replies
It schedules tasks to run at fixed times of the day
It logs every SQL statement that the app executes
e:
Without it, an uncaught exception in a controller becomes a generic 500 error. With `@RestControllerAdvice` you write one class that catches exceptions from every controller and returns a clean JSON body with the right status code (404 for "not found", 400 for validation, 409 for conflicts...).
It keeps controllers free of try/catch and gives clients a predictable error format.
r: One @RestControllerAdvice class = consistent error responses.
fa: It centralizes exception handling for all controllers, converting exceptions into consistent HTTP error responses

q: How do you validate request data in Spring Boot?
o: Only with `if` statements repeated in every controller
Constraint annotations like `@NotBlank`, plus `@Valid`
With CSS rules that are applied on the client side
It is not possible to validate requests in Spring
e:
Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation) lets you declare rules on fields. Put `@Valid` before the `@RequestBody` parameter and Spring checks the rules before running your method. On failure it throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which you can convert to a 400 response.
The starter is `spring-boot-starter-validation`.
Never trust client data: validate on the server even if the front-end also validates.
r: @Valid + constraint annotations = declarative validation.
fa: Add Bean Validation annotations (`@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size`...) on the fields and use `@Valid` on the controller parameter

q: Why use DTOs instead of exposing JPA entities directly in your API?
o: DTOs always compile faster than the entities do
To control what the API exposes and keep it stable
Entities cannot be serialized to JSON in any way
Spring requires DTOs for every controller method
e:
A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a simple class (often a `record`) shaped for the API.
If you return an entity: you may leak sensitive fields, JSON serialization may trigger lazy loading (or fail), and any database change breaks your API contract.
With DTOs, the API and the database can evolve separately. Mapping is done by hand or with MapStruct.
r: Entity = database shape. DTO = API shape.
fa: To control exactly what leaves/enters the API (no password hashes or internal fields), avoid lazy-loading surprises and keep the API stable when the database changes

q: Which test annotation starts the FULL Spring application context, and which loads only the web layer?
o: `@WebMvcTest` starts the full context; `@SpringBootTest` loads the web layer
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full context; `@WebMvcTest` loads the web layer
Both annotations always load the whole application context
`@DataJpaTest` starts the full context of the application
e:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application: slow but realistic (integration tests).
Test slices load only the part you are testing, so they are faster:
- `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)`: only the web layer; you mock services and call endpoints with `MockMvc`.
- `@DataJpaTest`: only JPA and repositories, with an in-memory database by default.
For pure unit tests of a service, skip Spring: use JUnit + Mockito.
r: Slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) are fast; @SpringBootTest is the full app.
fa: `@SpringBootTest` is full; `@WebMvcTest` loads only controllers and web components (with MockMvc)

q: What is Mockito used for in tests?
o: Running the application in a production environment
Creating mocks for dependencies to test a class alone
Compiling Java source files into bytecode quickly
Managing database schema migrations between versions
e:
Mockito creates fake versions of your dependencies. You tell the mock what to return (`when(...).thenReturn(...)`) and later verify calls (`verify(...)`).
This lets you test `OrderService` without a real database or payment provider.
With JUnit 5: `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`, `@Mock` for fakes and `@InjectMocks` for the class under test.
r: Mockito = fake dependencies for isolated unit tests.
fa: Creating mock objects that stand in for real dependencies, so you test one class in isolation and verify its interactions

q: How does a request flow through Spring MVC?
o: The browser calls the controller method straight away
`DispatcherServlet` maps the request to a controller
The database receives the request first and forwards it
The request is stored in a queue and processed later
e:
1. The embedded servlet container (Tomcat) receives the HTTP request.
2. Filters run (security, logging).
3. The `DispatcherServlet` is the single entry point: it finds which controller method handles that URL and HTTP method.
4. Arguments are resolved (`@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody` via Jackson) and the controller runs, calling services and repositories.
5. The return value is converted (usually to JSON) and written to the response; exceptions go to `@ControllerAdvice`.
r: Tomcat, filters, DispatcherServlet, controller, service, repository.
fa: The embedded server (Tomcat) receives it, the `DispatcherServlet` (front controller) maps it to a controller method, which calls services; the result is converted to JSON and returned

q: What does Spring Security do by default when you just add the starter?
o: Nothing: you must configure every rule yourself first
It secures all endpoints, with a generated password
It encrypts the whole database with a default key
It blocks only POST requests and leaves GET open
e:
Adding `spring-boot-starter-security` is "secure by default": every endpoint needs authentication, a default user `user` is created with a random password printed in the log, and CSRF protection is on for browser-style requests.
You then define a `SecurityFilterChain` bean to say which URLs are public, how users authenticate (JWT, OAuth2, form login) and which roles can do what.
Store passwords hashed with `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, never in plain text.
r: Spring Security: filter chain, authn then authz, BCrypt for passwords.
fa: Secures all endpoints (login form / HTTP Basic with a generated password) until you define your own rules

q: What is JDBC?
o: A JavaScript library for building database dashboards
The standard low-level Java API for running SQL
A Java build tool that packages the applications
A web framework that is used to build REST services
e:
JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) lets Java talk to any relational database through a driver: open a `Connection`, create a statement, run SQL and read the `ResultSet`.
JPA/Hibernate and Spring's `JdbcTemplate` are built on top of JDBC.
Always use `PreparedStatement` with `?` parameters and never concatenate user input into SQL (that is SQL injection).
r: JDBC = Java to SQL database. Always PreparedStatement.
fa: The standard low-level Java API to connect to relational databases and run SQL

q: What is a servlet and a servlet container (like Tomcat)?
o: A servlet handles HTTP requests; Tomcat runs servlets
A servlet is a database server; Tomcat is a build tool
A servlet is a JavaScript function run in the browser
A servlet is a test file; Tomcat compiles Java code
e:
A servlet is a Java class that receives an HTTP request and writes a response. It is the base technology of Java web applications.
A servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) is the server that listens on a port, parses HTTP, manages threads and calls your servlets.
Spring MVC is built on one servlet, the `DispatcherServlet`. Classic apps were packaged as WAR files and deployed in a Tomcat; Spring Boot embeds Tomcat inside a runnable JAR.
r: Servlet = Java HTTP handler. Container = the server that runs it.
fa: A servlet is a small Java class that handles HTTP requests; a container such as Tomcat runs servlets, receives the HTTP traffic and calls the right servlet

q: What is Jackson and what happens in `@RestController` when a method returns an object?
o: Jackson is a test runner, so the returned object is ignored
Jackson is the default JSON library for converting objects
Jackson encrypts the returned data before sending it out
Jackson is a database where the object gets stored later
e:
Jackson (`ObjectMapper`) serializes Java objects to JSON and deserializes JSON to Java objects. Spring Boot includes it with the web starter.
Useful annotations: `@JsonIgnore` (hide a field), `@JsonProperty("user_name")` (rename), `@JsonFormat` (date format).
Common issue: serializing a JPA entity with bidirectional relations can loop forever; DTOs avoid it.
r: Jackson = Java object to/from JSON.
fa: Jackson is the default JSON library: Spring uses it to convert the returned object to JSON (and request JSON to objects)

q: What is Spring Boot Actuator?
o: A UI framework that is used to build web pages
A module with health, metrics and info endpoints
A code generator that creates the controllers
A database driver for the relational databases
e:
Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and you get endpoints to see how the app is doing: `/actuator/health` (is it up? is the database reachable?), `/actuator/metrics`, `/actuator/info`.
Orchestrators like Kubernetes call the health endpoint for liveness and readiness probes. Metrics integrate with Prometheus/Micrometer.
Expose only what you need and protect the rest: some endpoints reveal sensitive details.
r: Actuator = health and metrics endpoints for operations.
fa: A module exposing operational endpoints such as `/actuator/health`, metrics and info, used for monitoring and Kubernetes probes

q: What is Spring AOP (aspect-oriented programming) typically used for?
o: Writing the HTML templates for the views of an app
Adding logging or security around methods without edits
Compiling the project faster with fewer classes
Storing the user sessions between two requests
e:
Some concerns appear in many places (logging, transactions, security checks, metrics). Copying that code into every method clutters the logic.
AOP lets you define an aspect (advice) and where it applies (pointcut). Spring implements it with proxies that wrap your beans: `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async` and method security all work this way.
Because it is proxy-based, calls inside the same class are not intercepted (self-invocation).
r: AOP = reusable behavior around methods, implemented with proxies.
fa: Adding cross-cutting behavior such as logging, transactions, security or timing around methods without changing their code, using proxies

q: Spring Boot 3 requires which Java version at minimum, and what package rename happened?
o: Java 8 as the minimum; no package change at all
Java 17; `javax.*` packages became `jakarta.*`
Java 11 as the minimum; `java.*` became `jdk.*`
Java 21 as the minimum; `spring.*` became `boot.*`
e:
Spring Boot 3 (Spring Framework 6) requires Java 17 or newer.
It also moved from Java EE to Jakarta EE 9+, so imports changed from `javax.persistence.*`, `javax.servlet.*`, `javax.validation.*` to `jakarta.persistence.*`, `jakarta.servlet.*`, `jakarta.validation.*`.
If you migrate an old project (Boot 2.x), this rename is the most common breaking change.
r: Boot 3 = Java 17+ and jakarta.* imports.

q: What is the difference between `@RequestParam` and `@PathVariable`?
o: They are identical; both read the value from the URL
`@PathVariable` is from the path; `@RequestParam` the query
`@RequestParam` is meant for reading JSON bodies only
`@PathVariable` can only be used on POST requests
e:
Path variables identify a specific resource: `/users/{id}`.
Query parameters filter, sort or paginate a collection: `/users?role=admin&page=2`.
Both are bound to method parameters. `@RequestParam` can be optional with a default: `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page`.
r: Path = which resource. Query = how to filter/sort it.
fa: `@PathVariable` takes a value from the URL path (`/users/42`); `@RequestParam` takes it from the query string (`/users?role=admin`)

q: Explain Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection, and why Spring uses them.
a:
- Inversion of Control: your code no longer controls the creation and lifecycle of its collaborators; a container does.
- Dependency Injection is the way IoC is applied: a class declares dependencies (constructor parameters) and the container supplies them.
- Spring scans for beans (`@Component`, `@Service`...), builds the object graph at startup and injects dependencies.
- Benefits: loose coupling (depend on interfaces), easy testing with mocks, central configuration, lifecycle management.
- Example: `OrderService(PaymentGateway g)`; in production Spring gives a Stripe gateway, in tests you pass a mock.

q: Walk me through building a REST endpoint in Spring Boot, from request to database.
a:
- Controller (`@RestController`): maps the URL, reads input (`@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody` with `@Valid`), returns a DTO and the right status (`ResponseEntity`).
- Service (`@Service`): business rules and `@Transactional` boundaries.
- Repository (`JpaRepository`): database access; entity with `@Entity`.
- Error handling: `@RestControllerAdvice` turns exceptions into 400/404/409 responses.
- Config: `application.yml`, profiles, secrets from environment variables.
- Tests: unit tests with Mockito for services, `@WebMvcTest` for controllers, `@DataJpaTest` or Testcontainers for repositories.
- Ops: Actuator health endpoint, structured logs.

q: What are the most common pitfalls with JPA/Hibernate and `@Transactional`?
a:
- N+1 queries: LAZY collections accessed in a loop; fix with `join fetch`, `@EntityGraph`, batch size or DTO projections.
- `LazyInitializationException`: reading a lazy field outside the transaction; fetch what you need inside the service or use DTOs.
- Self-invocation or private methods: proxy bypassed, so no transaction.
- Checked exceptions do not roll back by default (`rollbackFor`).
- Too-long transactions (calling slow HTTP services inside) hold database connections.
- Returning entities directly from controllers: leaks fields and triggers lazy loading.
- `open-in-view` (default true in Boot) hides lazy loading problems in the web layer; many teams disable it.

q: Spring vs Spring Boot vs Spring MVC vs Spring Data: what is each?
a:
- Spring Framework: core container (IoC/DI), AOP, transactions and the base of everything.
- Spring MVC: the web module: controllers, `DispatcherServlet`, request mapping, JSON conversion.
- Spring Data: simplifies data access (JPA, MongoDB, Redis...) with repository interfaces.
- Spring Security: authentication and authorization.
- Spring Boot: opinionated layer that auto-configures all of the above, adds starters, embedded server and Actuator.
- In one line: Spring is the toolbox, Spring Boot is the pre-assembled workshop.

q: What is an annotation such as `@Override` or `@Service` in Java?
o: A label (metadata) on code that the compiler or a framework reads
A comment that the compiler and frameworks always ignore
A mandatory import statement placed at the top of the file
A kind of loop that repeats over a list
e:
Annotations start with `@` and sit above classes, methods or fields.
Example: `@Override` tells the compiler to check that the method really overrides a parent method. `@Service` tells Spring to create and manage an object of that class.
Spring uses annotations everywhere, so reading them is a core skill: `@RestController`, `@GetMapping`, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional`.
r: Annotation = a label that frameworks read.
fa: A label (metadata) attached to code that the compiler or a framework reads to change how it behaves

q: In Spring, what is a 'bean'?
o: An object created and managed by the Spring container
A kind of database used for caching Spring objects
A Java keyword that marks any class as injectable
A test file that checks the Spring configuration
e:
The Spring documentation: a bean is an object that is instantiated, assembled and managed by a Spring IoC container.
Instead of writing `new OrderService()` everywhere, you let Spring create one and give it to the classes that need it (dependency injection).
Classes marked with `@Component`, `@Service` or `@Repository` become beans.
r: Bean = an object managed by Spring.
fa: An object that is created, assembled and managed by the Spring container

q: What is Apache Tomcat, and why do Spring Boot web apps often include it?
o: An open source Java web server, embeddable in Boot
A database engine that is bundled with Spring Boot
A cloud provider that hosts Spring Boot applications
A build tool that packages Spring Boot applications
e:
A Java web app needs a server that listens for HTTP requests and passes them to your code.
Tomcat is that kind of server. In the old style you installed Tomcat and deployed a WAR file into it.
Spring Boot can embed Tomcat (or Jetty or Undertow) inside your application, so there is nothing to install: you run the JAR and the server starts.
r: Tomcat = the web server inside most Spring Boot apps.
fa: An open source web server for Java (an implementation of Jakarta Servlet and related specifications) that Spring Boot can embed so your app starts with `java -jar`

q: A Spring Boot web app starts with default settings. On which port does the embedded server listen?
e:
The Spring Boot reference says that by default the embedded server listens for HTTP requests on port 8080. The Spring quickstart opens `http://localhost:8080/hello`.
You can change it with `server.port=9090` in `application.properties`.
For comparison: HTTP normally uses 80 and HTTPS 443.
r: Spring Boot default port: 8080.

q: What is `application.properties` (or `application.yml`) in a Spring Boot project?
o: The configuration file with the port and database URL
The main Java class that starts up the application
The Maven repository where dependencies are stored
The test report that is generated after the build
e:
Spring Boot reads settings from this file in `src/main/resources`, so you can change behavior without changing code.
Examples: `server.port=9090`, `spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop`.
Different environments can use different files (profiles), and secrets should come from environment variables, not from a committed file.
r: application.properties = settings of the app.
fa: The configuration file where you set values such as the server port or the database URL

q: What are JPA (Jakarta Persistence) and Hibernate?
o: JPA is a mapping specification; Hibernate implements it
Both are web servers that are used to run Java apps
JPA is a database engine; Hibernate is its backup tool
JPA is a testing tool; Hibernate is a build system
e:
An ORM (object-relational mapper) lets you work with Java objects instead of writing SQL for every operation: it converts objects to rows and back.
JPA defines the standard API (annotations like `@Entity`, `@Id`). Hibernate is software that implements it.
JPA was called Java Persistence API; since the move to Jakarta EE it is Jakarta Persistence, and the package changed from `javax.persistence` to `jakarta.persistence`.
r: JPA = the standard. Hibernate = the implementation.
fa: JPA is a specification for mapping Java objects to database tables; Hibernate is a popular implementation of it (an ORM)

q: What is start.spring.io (Spring Initializr)?
o: A web tool that generates a Spring Boot project
A Spring-only database used for local testing
The test runner that ships with Spring Boot
A paid cloud service that hosts Spring apps
e:
You choose options (build tool such as Maven or Gradle, language, Spring Boot version, dependencies like 'Spring Web'), click Generate, and download a zip with a working project: `pom.xml`, the main class and the folder structure.
The official Spring quickstart starts exactly like this. IDEs such as IntelliJ also have it built in.
r: Initializr = project generator for Spring Boot.
fa: A web tool that generates a ready-to-run Spring Boot project skeleton with the dependencies you choose
